The manipulation of time in this excerpt (which is the opening of Stefan Zweig's famous novella *Der Amokläufer*) is masterfully balanced to set up the narrative frame and build atmosphere. 

First, the author uses **compression of time** to bridge the gap between the "present" of the narrator (years after 1912) and the inciting incident in March 1912, quickly summarizing the aftermath of the accident in Naples in a single paragraph to hook the reader's curiosity. He then jumps back in time to Calcutta, compressing a two-day process of booking a ticket and boarding the ship into just a few sentences ("Am nächsten Tage..."). 

Once the narrator is aboard the ship, the pacing shifts toward **stretching of time** (or slowing the narrative pace) through detailed sensory descriptions of the cramped, stifling cabin. By lingering on the smell of oil and mold and the relentless whirring of the fan, the writer effectively slows down the story time to make the reader feel the narrator's claustrophobia and set the oppressive mood required for the remainder of the story.
